messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan had always found a quiet solitude in the walk home from his studio. The late-night emptiness of the industrial district, the echo of his own footsteps under the overpass—it was a space for his mind to unspool after a day at the canvas. That changed six months ago. Two figures emerged from the deep shadows of the concrete supports, their movements sudden and sharp. He remembered the glint of something metallic, a rough hand on his shoulder, and a voice demanding his wallet and phone. The event itself is a blur in his mind, a collection of disjointed sensory snapshots rather than a coherent narrative. When he tries to deliberately recall the sequence of events, he finds the memory slippery and hard to grasp, as if key pieces are simply missing.

In the weeks that followed, the missing pieces began to torment him. Fragments of the memory would surface without warning—the smell of stale urine in the underpass, the specific scrape of a shoe on gravel. Each time a piece returned, it brought with it a hot, searing guilt for not having fought back, for freezing, for being so unaware. This guilt solidified into a new, rigid understanding of the world: he couldn't rely on other people for safety, and more than that, people were fundamentally not to be trusted. This conviction began to color everything. He felt a profound sense of being set apart from others, as if he now carried a dark knowledge that they didn't, which left him feeling utterly isolated, even from his wife. The memory of his own helplessness fed this belief that he was alone in his own protection.

The city, once his muse, transformed into a landscape of potential threats. The underpass near his studio became an impossible route, a spatial trigger that would cause his chest to tighten and his body to flood with adrenaline. Just seeing it from a distance was enough to make him feel tense and keyed up for the rest of the day. Each time he had to detour around it, the thought would land with the force of a conviction: the world was no longer a place he could move through freely, and other people were the reason why. This constant state of being on alert meant he was always scanning his surroundings, his eyes darting to anyone who walked too quickly or stood too long in a doorway. His wife noticed his irritability first, the way he would snap over a misplaced set of keys or a sudden noise, his anger a brittle shield against a danger only he could see. He had come to believe that this vigilance was the only thing keeping him safe, a necessary armor built from the certainty that people were untrustworthy.

The cycle has become suffocating, a self-fueling engine of fear. Waking in a sweat from a nightmare leaves a residue of terror that primes his body for immediate danger, his muscles coiled and ready to react. This state of high alert makes him exquisitely sensitive to his environment, turning the mundane—a car backfiring, a stranger’s sudden laugh—into a trigger that brings an intrusive flash of memory. These flashes, in turn, reinforce his deeply held belief that the world is a dangerous place and he is alone in it, which only serves to heighten his need to scan for danger. Even his own thoughts have become triggers; his mistrust of others now makes him interpret neutral interactions as potentially hostile, which can then spark a memory of the attack, creating a loop where his internal state and the external world continuously confirm his worst fears.

His work as a painter, his life’s passion, has suffered immensely. He can no longer lose himself in the canvas. Instead, he spends hours at his studio window, tracking the movements of people on the street below. The physical location of his studio, once a haven, now feels like a liability, a constant, unavoidable reminder of the nearby underpass. He has pulled away from friends, unable to explain the chasm that has opened between his experience and theirs. It was after he yelled at his wife for startling him when she brought him a cup of tea in the studio that he finally made the call. The look of fear and hurt in her eyes was a reflection of a man he didn't recognize. Rohan came to therapy because he feels he is losing his marriage and himself, desperate to find a way to feel safe enough to put down his armor, even for a moment.
